text: RBAC organizes access into roles, least privilege keeps each role narrow, segregation of duties stops one person controlling a whole process. All three are preventive. Access reviews are detective, the recurring check that catches whatever slipped through anyway.

The defining feature of a real access review isn't that someone runs a report, it's who signs off on what the report shows. IT can generate a list of everyone with access to the Customers table in minutes. What takes a real process is getting the data owner to look at that list, person by person, and attest, yes this person still needs it, or no, remove it. IT usually can't judge whether access is still needed, only the business owner knows whether someone's still on the project that justified the grant eighteen months ago.

Most organizations run certifications quarterly for the most sensitive systems, annually for lower-risk ones. But certain events should trigger an unscheduled review too: a role change, confirming the old access is actually gone. A new regulation or audit finding naming a specific system. A security incident involving the system. A merger or reorganization that changes who should have access to what.

Finding a problem is only half the process. Remediation is the actual removal or correction of flagged access, tracked with the same rigor as the review itself, who owns it, by what date, who confirms it happened. A review that flags ten stale grants and closes zero of them isn't a control, it's a to-do list that never gets done.
That closes out the preventive and detective controls in this chapter. Next up: privileged access, where the highest-risk accounts get the strictest version of everything covered so far.
